title: Vampire Planet: Inside China’s Coal Boom
author: Joshua Frank
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/sam-
bark-R1GWSOJ9cng-
unsplash-680x453.jpg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/09/04/vampire-planet-
the-china-coal-boom/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/sam-
bark-R1GWSOJ9cng-unsplash-680x453.jpg)

Image by Sam Bark.

Every time I write about China’s dirty energy consumption, there’s bound to be
a reader or two who thinks I’m picking a fight. They say China is making major
gains in renewables and that it’s only burning fossil fuels for now because
the economy is still growing. If anything, these critics point the finger at
the West, which consumes the goods China produces. So it’s the West’s fault,
not the fact that China is (by choice) an integral part of the global
capitalist economy.

Yes, China is rolling out renewables at an amazing pace. There’s no denying
it. And as far as individual consumption is concerned, the average person in
the US burns a hell of a lot more fossil fuels, and the West is overwhelmingly
responsible for getting us in this mess. The rub, however, is that, on a
country-wide scale, China is now by far the largest contributor of fossil fuel
emissions (roughly [one-third](https://www.iea.org/reports/an-energy-sector-
roadmap-to-carbon-neutrality-in-china/executive-summary) of global fossil fuel
and industrial CO2 emissions), and its government (not a typical Chinese
citizen) plays an outsized role, directly dictating how its economy operates.

That might not sit well with the pro-China crowd, but that’s a fact. Another
fact is that, when it comes to climate chaos, our atmosphere doesn’t give a
shit about where those emissions come from. The result is the same, and the
world pays the price. Even so, China's continued reliance on coal deserves a
little nuance, so let’s get into the numbers a bit.

According to a [July report](https://globalenergymonitor.org/article/china-
wasted-enough-wind-and-solar-cover-all-new-power-demand-h1-2026) by the Centre
for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) and Global Energy Monitor (where I
once worked as a researcher), China added 30 GW of new coal-fired electricity
capacity in the first half of 2026. It retired only 2.7 GW during the same
period, meaning China added a net 27.3 GW of coal-fired generating capacity to
its growing mix. [![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/06/Screen-
Shot-2026-08-21-at-11.06.12-AM.png)](https://www.pilsencommunitybooks.com/item/UfU8gx4LO98oZP-
hvrl3zQ)

It’s the highest first half-year China has experienced since 2016. At the same
time, the report estimates that China curtailed about 360 TWh of wind and
solar generation in the first half of 2026, including unreported curtailment.
Curtailment is just another word for "didn't use."

There’s more bad news. China has another 274 GW of coal power in the pipeline,
which would account for 22% of its current coal-powered fleet. In short, the
sheer scale of that pipeline risks locking in an enormous amount of future
dirty coal capacity even as China’s renewables expand.

Because China’s existing energy contracts prioritize coal-fired electricity,
renewables may be pushed out of the country's energy market. Add China's
insufficient grid flexibility, transmission capability, and storage, and you
have a recipe for a lot more wasted green energy and a clear advantage for its
massive coal fleet.

“China’s coal buildout is a warning about overcapacity, not a blueprint for
energy security. Coal capacity is still growing because of legacy approvals
and policy protections, even as plants run fewer hours and large volumes of
clean electricity go unused,” explains Qi Qin, China analyst at CREA. “The
answer is to reward genuine reliability, not to protect coal in both the
capacity and energy markets, which pushes out the clean power generation that
is the only viable path to genuine energy sovereignty.”

In short, China isn't just building new coal plants as backup for its
electricity grid. It's currently generating more coal power than it did last
year while also building so much additional capacity that the overall use of
its coal fleet is actually declining. It’s a wild situation.

We’re not picking on an emerging economy here, like India. We’re talking about
China, which generates almost [20%](https://www.foreignaffairs.com/china/next-
global-economic-crisis-made-china-michael-froman) of global economic output
and is the world’s largest economy by purchasing power. China is also the
world’s second-largest economy by nominal GDP, only behind the US.

By these metrics, China is not part of the Global South but a powerhouse in
the global capitalist system, even if many of its domestic policies (if you
aren’t counting its [mass surveillance](https://www.hrw.org/tag/mass-
surveillance-china)) are admired by some of the Western left.

There’s something not so unique to capitalist economies (state-run or not)
going on here. China’s energy demand is growing right along with its economy.
Coal, while still a hefty part of the country’s overall energy use, isn’t as
dominant as it once was. The caveat is that, despite China building out more
capacity, its coal-fired power generation fell slightly in 2025.

That distinction matters. China can build many more coal plants without using
the electricity they can produce. Whether they do so or not, however, is a
matter of choice, not of ability. China, for instance, burns more than [10
times](https://www.worldometers.info/coal/coal-consumption-by-country/) as
much coal every year as the United States, and with more plants being built,
that number could well grow.

If there’s a silver lining, it’s that despite building out all this coal
power, the IEA expects China’s coal demand to slightly decline through 2030.
Of course, as the world burns and floods, this is not fast enough.

Despite its increased capacity, coal-fired electricity generation
[fell](https://www.iea.org/reports/global-energy-
review-2026/coal?utm_source=chatgpt.com) 1.5% last year (coal demand for all
industries [grew](https://www.iea.org/reports/global-energy-
review-2026/coal?utm_source=chatgpt.com) by 0.1%). The hope, at least, is that
even if China builds more coal plants (which it is), it won’t need to use
them.

Right now, the story is about which energy sources China opts to tap, which
could all be complicated by the country’s data center boom. While still
[trailing](https://finance.yahoo.com/sectors/technology/articles/china-
throw-300-billion-data-141555218.html) the US’s data center rollout, China is
increasing its investment and building out more data centers, increasing
demand for electricity just like we're doing here in the US. A recent Wood
Mackenzie estimate reported that China could consume about [774 TWh annually
by 2030](https://www.woodmac.com/ja/press-releases/chinas-ai-boom-to-drive-
data-centre-power-demand-to-774-twh-by-2030/?utm_source=chatgpt.com), roughly
four times its current electricity consumption from data centers.

We'll have to wait and see how this pans out, but in the meantime, we have
every right to be concerned about where this could head.

+++
